text: Before opening the AWS console at all, it's worth sketching the plan in plain English. This lesson is about naming exactly which services do what, and just as importantly, which ones this project deliberately leaves out.

Here's the full chain. Raw order CSVs are already sitting in S3, in the northfield-raw-zone bucket. A Glue Crawler scans those files and infers their schema — column names and data types — without being told in advance. That schema becomes a table definition in the Glue Data Catalog, which is metadata only; it points at the files in S3, it doesn't copy them. And then Athena runs real SQL directly against those files, on demand, whenever someone asks a question.

Athena is worth pausing on. It's serverless — there's no cluster to spin up, no server to patch, nothing running while nobody's asking a question. You're billed per terabyte of data scanned, per query. For a single ad hoc question against a month of CSV files, that's about as close to zero fixed cost as AWS gets.

It's worth naming the next step up too, because this is exactly the kind of tradeoff an interviewer will ask about. A Glue ETL job would clean and reshape this data into a separate curated zone. Redshift would hold it for fast, repeated queries from multiple analysts. Both are real, more capable, and more expensive — and they earn that cost once there's a recurring workload, not for one question asked once.

So here's what done looks like for this plan. By the end of Lesson 6, there's a working Glue Crawler that has cataloged the raw files into a real table, and a simple SELECT star query in Athena proving the whole chain works end to end. Lesson 7 is where that chain actually answers the Operations Manager's real question.
With the plan sketched, next lesson confirms exactly what's sitting in that S3 bucket right now — the bucket name, the prefix, and the files themselves — before the Glue Crawler ever points at them.
